title: Scales on the Guitar
intro: A scale on the guitar is a pattern of frets in one hand position, repeated across the strings. Because shapes move, one pattern gives the scale in every key. The pentatonic boxes and the major-scale positions are the two systems every guitarist learns.

blocks.text: The minor pentatonic (see Other Scales (#/arts/music-theory/scales-and-keys/other-scales)) has five notes, so in one position each string gets exactly two. The first and best-known 'box' of A minor pentatonic sits at frets 5–8: strings 6 and 1 at frets 5 and 8, strings 5, 4 and 3 at 5 and 7, string 2 at 5 and 8. The roots (A) are at string 6 fret 5, string 4 fret 7 and string 1 fret 5.

widget.title: A minor pentatonic, box 1 (frets 5–8), up and down

blocks.alt: The neck from the nut to fret 17 with every note of A minor pentatonic (A C D E G) as a labelled dot, the A's in red, and brackets under the neck marking box 1 (frets 5 to 8) through box 5 (frets 14 to 17).
blocks.caption: A minor pentatonic over the whole neck, divided into its five boxes. Each box overlaps the next; box 1 is the familiar one at the 5th fret.

blocks.text: The same five notes continue up the neck in four more boxes, each starting on the next note of the scale; box 2 runs from fret 7 to 10, box 3 from 9 to 13, box 4 from 12 to 15, box 5 from 14 to 17, and then box 1 repeats at fret 17 (an octave up). Together they cover the whole neck. Read as C major pentatonic, box 1 is the same notes with C as the root: relative major and minor share the boxes.

Seven-note scales need three notes on some strings. A common one-position fingering of G major with the root on string 6 fret 3 covers frets 2–5: string 6 frets 2-3-5, string 5 frets 2-3-5, string 4 frets 2-4-5, string 3 frets 2-4-5, string 2 frets 3-5, string 1 frets 2-3-5. Slid up two frets it is A major.

items: CAGED positions: five major-scale fingerings, one around each CAGED chord shape (next page), covering the neck the same way as the five pentatonic boxes.
Three-notes-per-string (3NPS): exactly three notes on every string, seven patterns. Even for alternate picking and fast legato; the stretches are wider.

Modes: the same fingerings with a different note treated as the root. The G major pattern above, played over an A drone, is A Dorian; over C it is C Lydian (see The Modes (#/arts/music-theory/scales-and-keys/modes)).

blocks.title: Move the box
blocks.text: Where is box 1 of E minor pentatonic, and of C minor pentatonic?
solution: Box 1 starts with the root on string 6. E is open string 6 (and fret 12): box 1 at frets 0–3 (open position) or 12–15. C is string 6 fret 8: box 1 at frets 8–11.
blocks.answer: E: open position (or frets 12–15); C: frets 8–11

blocks.title: Relative
blocks.text: Which major pentatonic uses exactly the same frets as A minor pentatonic box 1?
solution: Relative major of A minor is C major: C major pentatonic (C D E G A) has the same five notes, with its root inside box 1 on string 3 fret 5 and string 1 fret 8 (and string 6 fret 8).

blocks.text: Sources: Goodrick, M. (1987). The Advancing Guitarist. Hal Leonard; Leavitt, W. G. (1966–1971). A Modern Method for Guitar, vols. 1–3. Berklee Press; Tagliarino, B. (2006). Guitar Fretboard Workbook. Hal Leonard; Levine, M. (1995). The Jazz Theory Book. Sher Music.
